thread.title: Dow Drops 76 Points Because the Market's Still Searching for Answers

title: Dow Drops 76 Points Because the Market's Still Searching for Answers
text:
Dow Drops 76 Points Because the Market’s Still Searching for Answers By Dec. 28, 2018 5:08 p.m. ET Order Reprints Michael Haddad Text size
Clueless. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 failed to hold their early-day gains and closed in the red, while the Nasdaq Composite managed to stay in positive territory, if barely. Investors will have to hold their breath until they can get a clearer picture of corporate America from the upcoming fourth-quarter earnings reports. In today’s After the Bell , we... ...wonder what’s a reasonable trading range — or the “new norm” — going forward; ...look into what’s needed for the market to resume its long-term uptrend; ...and ponder the headwinds and tailwinds for that to happen.
New Blood Needed
The market went on a mini roller-coaster ride on Friday, coming to a rest not far from where it started. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 76.42 points, or 0.3%, to 23,062.4, while the S&P 500 finished down 3.1 points, or 0.1%, at 2485.73 and the Nasdaq Composite edged up 5.03 points, or 0.1%, to 6584.52.
After December’s violent drop and this Wednesday’s unusual 5% rally, the market now seems to be struggling which direction to go next. There are both bullish and bearish voices prevailing the market.
Tom Essaye from the Sevens Report believes a trading range between 2550 and 2760 would likely be reasonable for the S&P 500 in the near term, calling it a “fair” value in the current macro environment. That is based on the expected earnings-per-share for S&P 500 companies, which is now at $171 for 2019, according to FactSet data, and assumes the market will be trading at 15-16 times price-to-earnings ratio. “The downside of that range accounts for real slowing growth and reduced earnings growth,” writes Essaye on Friday.
The Fed’s not-dovish-enough message and fear of a recession has helped push stocks below that 2550 lower bound lately, but that means the market is now at a discounted price and still have some space to rise, according to Essaye.
For the long-term, though, Nicholas Colas from DataTrek argues that the market needs some new blood in the system in order to start seeing better long run returns.
“Recall the reason why the S&P 500 has managed reasonable gains over the last 10 years: Amazon (AMZN), Google, Facebook (FB), Apple (AAPL), and Microsoft (MSFT) top the list,” writes Colas. “And even then, their performance only got us to a subpar 20-year track record...Imagine if they had not been in the mix.” It will be hard to see these companies doubling their market cap again in the next 10 years, writes Colas, so “a fresh crop of disruptive tech companies” is needed for the market to revive again.
The good news is that venture capitals have been plowing money into some of these businesses and we’ll likely see quite a few of them going public in the next few years — including Uber, Airbnb, WeWork and Pinterest. But Colas also reminds that IPO windows are “notoriously fickle, so we may have to wait a while if current market volatility persists.”
